title: Psalm 123: Eyes on the Hand of the Master
summary: The psalmist lifts his eyes to the LORD enthroned in heaven and compares the people's watchfulness to servants watching their master's hand for a sign. Then the psalm becomes a plea: have mercy on us, for we have had more than enough of the scorn of the comfortable and the contempt of the proud.
story: Psalm 121 opened with eyes lifted to the hills; Psalm 123 opens with eyes lifted higher, to the one enthroned in heaven. After the gladness of arriving in Jerusalem in Psalm 122, this short psalm is a reminder that the people who go up to worship still live under pressure. The first verse speaks as one person, and the rest speaks as “we” and “us”, so a single voice leads the whole community in prayer. The Songs of Ascents regularly move between individual and communal voices this way. Psalm 123 names a need without resolving it, and Psalm 124 answers with a memory of deliverance: if the LORD had not been on our side.
historical: The heading has no author, only “A song of ascents”. The psalm gives no names or events, so its setting has to be inferred from its content. The complaint is not of armies or siege but of contempt and scorn from people who are at ease. Many scholars connect that with the period after the exile, when the small community that returned to Judah under Persian rule lived under the ridicule of better-placed neighbors. The book of Nehemiah records exactly that kind of mockery from Sanballat, Tobiah, and others when the walls of Jerusalem were being rebuilt in the mid-fifth century BC (Nehemiah 2:19; 4:1-4). Other interpreters think the psalm fits any time when Israel was weak and despised, and some note that its language would suit a lowly class within Israel mocked by wealthy and powerful countrymen. Because the psalm names no one, it has been sung in all those situations.
cultural:
The central picture comes from the ordinary life of a household with servants. A servant or slave in a wealthy home was expected to watch the master's hand: a gesture could summon, dismiss, assign a task, or give food and wages. Silent signals were common in ancient households, so watching the hand meant being ready and dependent. The psalm includes both a male servant with his master and a female servant with her mistress, the woman of the house who directed the household's women. Ancient readers would also have known that the hand which gives orders can also give bread, protection, and kindness. The psalm looks to God's hand for the second: mercy.

The people described in verse 4 as “the arrogant” and “the proud” translate words meaning those at ease, secure and untroubled, and those who are lofty. Scorn from the secure was a keen social wound in an honor-and-shame culture, where public standing was a large part of a person's or a people's life. To be mocked was to be diminished in everyone's eyes.
literary: Psalm 123 is a brief communal lament, only four verses long, and it is built on repetition in the stair-step manner of the Songs of Ascents. The word eyes appears four times in the Hebrew of verses 1 and 2, and the phrase “have mercy” three times in verses 2 and 3. Verses 3 and 4 then repeat “much contempt” and “much scorn”, and the Hebrew says literally that the people's soul is filled, sated, with contempt, as if they have eaten it until they can take no more. The poem turns on the word “until” in verse 2: the eyes remain on the LORD “until He shows us mercy.” The psalm does not say when that will be; it ends with the people still waiting.

outline.t: Eyes lifted to the One enthroned in heaven
Like servants watching the master's hand
Have mercy: we are filled with contempt

doctrines.note: Prayer here is mostly looking: attentive, dependent waiting on God, with a short, repeated plea. The psalm shows that a prayer can be complete without an answer yet in hand.
God is “the One enthroned in heaven,” above the proud who scorn his people. The contrast between his throne and their ease places the mockers' power in perspective: it is real, but it is not final.
The psalm treats contempt as a real suffering worth bringing to God, not a small thing to be brushed off. Humiliation and scorn are named honestly, and God is asked to act on them.

words.note: Chanan, to be gracious or show favor. It describes kindness given freely by someone with power to someone without it, which fits the psalm's picture of servant and master. It appears three times here, in “until He shows us mercy” and the double plea “Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy.” The same root lies behind the LORD's self-description as gracious in Exodus 34:6.

Buz, contempt. It means treating someone as worthless, looking down on them. The word appears twice, framing the complaint in verses 3 and 4. Proverbs uses the verb from the same root for despising wisdom or a neighbor; the psalm shows what being despised feels like from the inside.

Sha'anan, at ease or secure. It can describe the untroubled peace of the faithful (Isaiah 33:20 uses it for a quiet Jerusalem), but here it describes complacent people whose comfort makes them careless of others. The BSB renders it “the arrogant”. The irony is sharp: those who have ease use it to mock those who don't.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 123, so the link is thematic. In the Gospels, the cry for mercy rises again and again from people who had nothing else to offer: two blind men calling out to Jesus as Son of David for mercy (Matthew 9:27; 20:30), a Canaanite woman who said even the dogs eat the crumbs from their masters' table (Matthew 15:22-27), ten men with leprosy (Luke 17:13). Jesus answers them. He also took on himself the contempt the psalm describes: he was mocked by soldiers, passersby, and rulers at his trial and crucifixion (Mark 15:16-32). Hebrews says he endured the cross, disregarding its shame (Hebrews 12:2). And in him the servant's watching of the master's hand is met by a master who serves, who says he came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45).
questions: The servant watches the master's hand for a signal. What would it look like for you to pay that kind of attention to God in a normal day?
The psalm names contempt as a real suffering. Where have you felt scorned or looked down on, and where might you have been among those at ease who looked down on others?
The psalm ends with the people still waiting for mercy. How do you pray when there is no answer yet?
